strengths: Significance: The paper explores a useful, simple attention modification across classification, autoregressive image generation, and LLM adaptation. Reported gains include ImageNet ViT-S/16 accuracy improving from 74.04% to 75.69% and CIFAR-10 generation improving from 3.0224 to 3.0032 BPD with approximately 2.39× higher throughput.

Empirical analysis: The component ablations provide useful information beyond headline results. Tables 13 and 16 distinguish the contributions of the RBF kernel, locality, and top-k selection, and reveal meaningful accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. Experiments within Swin also help investigate the kernel beyond adding locality.

Presentation and reproducibility: The attention rule is straightforward to follow, and Appendix D supplies substantial training configurations, hardware details, generation batch sizes, and example evaluation prompts.

Limitations and ethics: Appendix A appropriately acknowledges the idealized theoretical setting and the auxiliary nature of the LLM integration. These are reasonable scope limitations. The impact statement is proportionate to this architectural contribution, and the manuscript raises no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—bounded-confidence claims do not follow from the implemented mechanism. A positional window followed by top-k selection can retain arbitrarily distant query–key pairs and need not disconnect the interaction graph. Consequently, the nontrivial representation-space cutoff asserted in Eq. (21) is not established. Appendix C.1 assumes persistent disconnected groups rather than demonstrating their emergence or persistence; absence of cross-group coupling alone does not ensure that their representations remain separated under arbitrary V. The acknowledged idealization does not resolve these logical gaps.

Soundness—the mean-field proof has additional substantive problems. Eq. (22) omits the row normalization of the implemented attention, while its claimed gradient-flow relationship to Eq. (23) is not derived for general Q and K or asymmetric, state-dependent top-k supports. Differentiating that energy generally introduces terms absent from the stated velocity field. Tangency to the sphere does not establish invariance of arbitrary cluster supports, as asserted after Eq. (27). The Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality imported in Eq. (31) also lacks a justification for the modified kernel. Thus the advertised multi-cluster convergence is unsupported even within the proposed theoretical model.

Originality and interpretation: On any fixed selected support, normalized RBF attention is exactly softmax_j(q_i^T k_j / sigma^2 - ||k_j||^2 / (2 sigma^2)), since the query-norm term cancels. The distinction from softmax attention is therefore a key-norm bias, scaling, and support selection—not elimination of softmax-style normalization. The paper should explain this equivalence and compare against matched temperature/key-norm and local dot-product controls. Without these comparisons or a valid new theoretical result, the claimed conceptual advance over existing kernel and sparse attention is insufficiently established.

Efficiency claims require verification. Appendix D.2.4 attributes the Swin FLOP reduction to an RBF decomposition that avoids expensive inner products, but exact pairwise squared distances still require dimension-wise pair interactions, and value aggregation remains necessary. Table 14 reports over 50% total FLOP reductions despite retaining the same windows and omitting additional sparsity; Table 3 reports roughly 30% reductions despite unchanged projections and MLPs. These figures need an auditable operation breakdown. Algorithm 1 also computes affinities before masking, so its stated linear-in-sequence implementation requires clarification. The O(NWd) interaction bound is reasonable when only window candidates are computed, but does not substantiate the reported whole-model savings.

Experimental attribution is incomplete. Table 13 lacks dot-product attention with the same local/top-k support; the full method is also worse than its no-top-k variant with Mixup/CutMix (95.20% versus 95.59%). Table 16 gives the best likelihood to dense RBF attention. These results support potential utility of the kernel, but do not establish that multi-cluster synchronization explains the gains. LLM comparisons likewise lack a matched auxiliary dot-product pathway or matched adaptation-capacity control.

Attention-sink evidence is insufficient for the causal claims. Figures 7 and 11 do not clearly specify aggregation across queries, heads, examples, and the two attention pathways, or compare against the LoRA-only baseline. Excluding initial tokens through a local mask mechanically reduces their attention in that branch; it does not demonstrate reduced collapse in the retained global branch or explain downstream improvements. Qualitative attention maps also do not establish representation-space convergence. Appendix E's identification of sinks with global consensus is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility and evaluation uncertainty remain material. Results lack repeated-run variation, leaving small gains difficult to assess. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify evaluation splits/sample counts, the sampled Flan-v2 subset and overlap checks, auxiliary projection initialization/sharing, or FLOP measurement methodology. Tables 7–9 additionally list '0.1/✗' drop-path settings without explaining how this fits the claim of identical training protocols. These ambiguities should be resolved before the empirical results can reliably support the broad conclusions.

strengths: Significance: The paper explores a useful design space combining distance-based attention, local windows, and selective sparsity. Reported gains span image classification, autoregressive generation, and adaptation of two language-model families. For example, Table 3 reports ImageNet improvements of 1.65–3.24 percentage points, and Table 5 reports improved CIFAR-10 likelihood with approximately 2.4× generation throughput.

Experimental analysis: The appendix includes meaningful component ablations, window-size sensitivity, and experiments within Swin's existing local-attention architecture. Tables 13 and 16 help distinguish the contributions of the distance kernel, locality, and top-k selection, including cases where removing a component improves performance.

Presentation and reproducibility: The core attention rule is understandable, with explicit equations and pseudocode. The appendix supplies substantial training hyperparameters, hardware information, and evaluation prompt examples.

Limitations and ethics: Appendix A appropriately acknowledges the idealized theoretical setting and the auxiliary-only integration into pretrained LLMs. The impact statement is reasonable for general architectural research; no specific unresolved ethical concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—clustering guarantees do not follow from the implemented mechanism. Spatial/causal windows and top-k selection do not impose a fixed confidence radius in representation space: top-k can retain arbitrarily distant candidates, and overlapping windows can remain globally connected. Consequently, the compact-support assertion in Eq. (21) and the decomposition into disconnected groups are not established. Appendix C.1 assumes fragmentation rather than proving its emergence. Moreover, block-diagonal coupling alone does not preserve distinct cluster locations independently of V: under Eq. (19), disconnected singleton clusters with V = -I all converge to zero. This directly contradicts the claimed spectrum-independent preservation of separation.

Soundness—the mean-field proof has additional substantive gaps. Equation (22) omits the row normalization used by the actual attention rule. With arbitrary Q and K and directed top-k supports, the kernel need not be symmetric, and its energy gradient is not generally the stated vector field. Tangency to the sphere and absence of current cross-cluster interactions do not establish forward invariance of the sets C_k. The Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality and convergence bounds in Eqs. (31)–(32) are transferred without establishing their applicability to this modified kernel. These are problems within the idealized analysis itself, beyond the honestly acknowledged gap to practical Transformers.

Soundness—central computation claims are inconsistent with the stated architecture. Appendix D.2.4 attributes Swin FLOP reductions exceeding 50% to replacing dot products with RBF distances while retaining the same windows and omitting top-k. However, squared Euclidean distances still require pairwise feature computations, and projections and MLPs remain unchanged. Similarly, Table 3 reduces ViT-B/16 from 17.61G to 12.03G, whereas the two quadratic attention products in a standard 12-layer, 196-token, width-768 ViT-B account for only about 0.71G multiply-adds. The reported reduction therefore needs an operation-level accounting or disclosure of additional architectural changes. Algorithm 1 also computes affinities before masking; achieving O(NWd) requires explicitly restricting their computation to window candidates.

Originality: The conceptual connection to bounded-confidence dynamics is potentially interesting, but the mathematical distinction from softmax attention is overstated. On any fixed selected support, normalized RBF attention is exactly softmax_j(q_i·k_j/σ² - ||k_j||²/(2σ²)), because the query-norm term cancels. Thus, the contribution combines a key-norm bias with familiar locality and top-k mechanisms. Stronger positioning against Gaussian/distance attention and a matched local dot-product-plus-top-k baseline are needed to isolate what is new and useful.

Experimental attribution remains incomplete. Table 13 lacks the matched local dot-product control, and its augmented setting performs better without top-k: 95.59% versus 95.20%, at identical reported FLOPs. Table 16 achieves the best likelihood without either locality or sparsity. These results support useful empirical effects but do not establish multi-cluster synchronization as their cause. For LLMs, adding a learnable auxiliary pathway also changes adaptation capacity; a comparable dot-product auxiliary pathway or parameter-matched adapter control is missing. No repeated-run variability is reported, limiting confidence in smaller improvements.

Attention-sink claims exceed the evidence. Representation consensus does not itself imply attention concentration on particular tokens; identical token representations can instead produce uniform attention. Figures 7 and 11 lack sufficient detail about query/head/sample aggregation and which pathway is measured. Because the LLM retains global attention, excluding initial tokens from the auxiliary local branch does not establish removal of sinks from the complete model. Quantitative representation-diversity measurements and comparison against the LoRA-finetuned baseline would strengthen the proposed mechanism.

Reproducibility and scope: The manuscript does not sufficiently specify evaluation splits/sample counts, selection and benchmark-overlap checks for the Flan-v2 subset, initialization or sharing of the added LLM projections, and FLOP-counting methodology. Tables 7–9 also contain unexplained '0.1/✗' drop-path entries despite claims of identical training protocols. Finally, the abstract's broad computational-savings claim needs qualification: the LLM variants retain quadratic global attention and are slightly slower in Table 19. The empirical promise is insufficient to overcome the unresolved theoretical and efficiency issues.

strengths: Significance: The reported improvements span several modalities and model sizes. For example, CIFAR-100 ViT-S accuracy increases from 71.74% to 77.05%, ImageNet ViT-S/16 improves from 74.04% to 75.69%, and CIFAR-10 generation improves from 3.0224 to 3.0032 BPD with approximately 2.4× higher throughput. These results motivate further investigation.

Originality: Connecting distance-based sparse attention to bounded-confidence dynamics is an interesting organizing perspective. Combining a learnable RBF kernel, local windows, and selective interactions yields a straightforward, potentially useful architectural variant.

Experimental analysis: Tables 13 and 16 investigate individual components, including informative cases where removing sparsity improves accuracy or likelihood. The Swin experiments also examine the RBF kernel within an already local architecture.

Presentation and limitations: The mechanism is clearly described through equations and pseudocode, and the appendix supplies substantial training details. Appendix A appropriately acknowledges the idealized theoretical setting and auxiliary-only LLM integration. The impact statement is proportionate; no specific material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—bounded-confidence claims: Positional windows and top-k selection do not impose a nontrivial fixed distance cutoff in representation space. Top-k can retain arbitrarily distant candidates, and overlapping local neighborhoods can remain globally connected. Consequently, the compact-support assertion in Eq. (21) and the claimed decomposition into independent clusters do not follow from the implemented mechanism. Appendix C.1 assumes disconnected groups and persistent separation rather than establishing their emergence or preservation.

Soundness—mean-field derivation: Eqs. (22)–(23) do not establish a gradient-flow representation of the proposed normalized attention. For general learned Q and K, the kernel is asymmetric, and differentiating its interaction energy does not produce the stated velocity field. The normalization in Eq. (12) is also absent. Tangency to the sphere alone does not imply invariance of separated cluster supports, and the subsequent convergence inequalities are imported without establishing their applicability. These are substantive gaps beyond the acknowledged finite-network limitations.

Soundness—efficiency accounting: Appendix D.2.4 attributes more than 50% lower Swin FLOPs to replacing dot products with an RBF kernel while preserving windows and omitting top-k. Squared Euclidean distance still requires comparable pairwise arithmetic, while projections and MLPs remain unchanged. Likewise, the roughly 30% whole-model ViT savings are difficult to reconcile with unchanged projections and MLPs, especially at short sequence lengths. An operation-level accounting and implementation are needed to validate these central efficiency results.

Originality and attribution: On any fixed support, normalized RBF attention is exactly softmax over q_i·k_j/σ² − ||k_j||²/(2σ²), since the query-norm term cancels. This equivalence substantially qualifies the contrast with softmax and global normalization. Comparisons against local dot-product attention, local top-k dot-product attention, and a learned-temperature/key-norm-bias baseline are needed to isolate the contribution. Existing ablations remove components from the RBF model but do not supply these controls.

Mechanistic evidence: Attention heatmaps do not establish representation-level multi-cluster convergence. Figures 7 and 11 also lack sufficient measurement detail to distinguish reduced sink attention in the retained global pathway from the direct effect of masking the first token in the auxiliary pathway. Representation-diversity measurements, branch-specific sink statistics, and a matched local-attention control would be needed to support the proposed causal explanation.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Results lack repeated-seed uncertainty, which matters for the smaller likelihood and language-benchmark gains. LLM evaluation split sizes, the precise Flan-v2 subset, and overlap filtering are insufficiently documented. The added pathway also changes trainable capacity and lacks a capacity-matched auxiliary-attention baseline. Its projection initialization and parameter sharing require clarification. Training tables help, but the manuscript does not provide enough implementation detail to resolve these issues.

Overall assessment: The empirical findings are promising, but the central theoretical justification and computational savings remain insufficiently supported. The LLM models retain global attention and show slight throughput reductions in Table 19, further limiting the broad efficiency claim. These material issues outweigh the current evidence for acceptance.
